title: Trump: Bannon: No one can know Manafort's still with us (and Hannity)
description_short: Trump: Bannon: No one can know Manafort's still with us (and Hannity)
description_medium: A 2016 email chain shows Paul Manafort telling Jared Kushner that he had spoken with Rick Gates, Sean Hannity, and Reince Priebus. Kushner forwarded the message to Steve Bannon, who replied that the campaign could not let it become public that Manafort was advising them. The memo Manafort mentioned is not included in the released material.
description_long: In a 2016 email chain later included among documents obtained during the Mueller investigation, Paul Manafort told Jared Kushner he had already spoken with Rick Gates, Sean Hannity, and Reince Priebus. The memo Manafort referenced is not available, so its contents are unknown. Kushner forwarded the message to David Bossie and Steve Bannon. Bannon replied that the team “can’t let word get out he is advising us.” The exchange came after Manafort resigned as campaign chair in August, when the public understood he was no longer involved in the campaign. The correspondence therefore records that campaign figures were concerned about disclosing his continued advice, but it does not show what advice he gave, whether he held a formal role, or what Donald Trump knew about the arrangement. It is an email record of campaign communications, not proof by itself of an illegal act. The episode’s significance lies in the gap between Manafort’s public departure and Bannon’s private description of him as an adviser, while the extent of that advice remains unspecified.
notes: Repair note: Replaced unrelated war and national-security tags with the people and campaign correspondence in the source.

title: Trump: McConnell and Rand Paul block sanctions on Kremlin company and Manafort business partner
description_short: Trump: McConnell and Rand Paul block sanctions on Kremlin company and Manafort business partner
description_medium: The Senate voted 57–42 on a measure to reinstate sanctions on Russian aluminum producer Rusal, three votes short of the 60 needed to advance it; the House had passed its measure 362–53. The company was co-owned by Oleg Deripaska, a Paul Manafort associate. Rusal later invested in a Kentucky aluminum project seeking Russian funding.
description_long: In January 2019, the Senate considered a measure to reinstate sanctions on Rusal, a Russian aluminum company co-owned by Oleg Deripaska, an associate of former Trump campaign chair Paul Manafort. The vote was 57–42, falling three short of the 60 votes needed to advance the measure; the House had approved a similar resolution 362–53. The linked account says Mitch McConnell campaigned against the Senate measure and identifies Rand Paul among the senators opposing it. The article also reports that a Rusal executive dined with Craig Bouchard, then chief executive of Kentucky-based Braidy Industries, which was seeking Russian financing for an aluminum mill. Within three months of the sanctions being lifted, Rusal began investing in the project, and the source says its investment reached at least $75 million by the end of 2019. The timing and business connections are relevant context, but they do not establish that the investment caused any senator’s vote or prove a personal benefit to McConnell or Paul. The event is a failed Senate effort to restore sanctions, followed by a reported investment relationship.
notes: Repair note: Replaced internal audit boilerplate and unrelated tariff tags with the vote, company, and investment details in the linked account.

title: Trump: Judge orders Donald Trump to pay $2m for illegal use of charity funds
description_short: Trump: Judge orders Donald Trump to pay $2m for illegal use of charity funds
description_medium: A New York judge ordered Donald Trump to pay $2 million in a settlement over misuse of Trump Foundation funds. Trump admitted that the foundation made illegal political contributions, promoted his campaign, paid business obligations, and gave his campaign control over about $2.8 million raised at a veterans’ fundraiser. The payment followed a civil case brought by the state attorney general.
description_long: In November 2019, a New York judge ordered Donald Trump to pay $2 million as part of a settlement concerning misuse of Trump Foundation funds. Trump made 19 admissions in the agreement, acknowledging that the foundation paid business obligations, supported his campaign, and made illegal political contributions. He also admitted that the foundation gave his presidential campaign control of about $2.8 million raised at a 2016 veterans’ fundraiser, which he acknowledged was a campaign event. The foundation had purchased a $10,000 portrait of Trump that was displayed at one of his Florida hotels, and it paid obligations connected to a golf club and Mar-a-Lago. The settlement resolved a case opened in June 2018 and imposed a payment smaller than the $8 million the attorney general had sought. These admissions and the court-ordered payment document misuse of charitable assets for political and business purposes. The settlement’s findings are distinct from a criminal conviction, and the source does not establish that every use of foundation funds was unlawful. Trump later denied that he had admitted wrongdoing.
notes: Repair note: Replaced internal audit boilerplate with the settlement admissions, amounts, and documented uses of foundation funds.

title: Trump: White supremacist gang member destroys property to stoke chaos in Minnesota
description_short: Trump: White supremacist gang member destroys property to stoke chaos in Minnesota
description_medium: Video from Minneapolis protests in May 2020 showed a man later identified as Mitchell Carlson breaking AutoZone windows and spray-painting “free shit for everyone.” A court affidavit said the person known as “Umbrella Man” appeared to have intended to incite violence. At the time of the report, police had not charged him.
description_long: During protests in Minneapolis following George Floyd’s murder in May 2020, video showed a person later identified as Mitchell Carlson breaking windows at an AutoZone and spray-painting “free shit for everyone.” A search-warrant affidavit quoted by the report said the actions preceded fires and looting and described the person known as “Umbrella Man” as appearing to have intended to incite violence. A subsequent investigation reportedly linked Carlson to the Aryan Cowboy Brotherhood, a white-supremacist prison and street gang. The report says police had not charged him as of October 2020. Those are investigative claims, not a court finding of guilt or motive. The incident concerns vandalism during protests and the later identification of a suspect; the cited material does not connect the event to Donald Trump. Its title’s prefix suggests a Trump-related event, while the account itself centers on Carlson, the vandalism, and investigators’ theory about incitement. A fuller entry needs evidence of the connection to Trump or a title that identifies the incident without implying one.
notes: Needs context: The linked report and search-warrant affidavit describe vandalism, an investigative theory about incitement, and a later gang association; police had not charged Carlson as of October 2020. The account does not connect the incident to Trump, as the title prefix implies, and no court has established the suspect’s guilt or motive.

Proposed correction: Remove the Trump prefix or provide evidence of a Trump connection; attribute the motive and gang affiliation to the investigative reporting rather than stating them as adjudicated facts.
Repair note: Replaced the unrelated immigration category tags with the protest, vandalism, suspect, and group described in the report.

title: Trump: Mark Meadows, Trump's Chief of Staff, and six others test positive for COVID-19
description_short: Trump: Mark Meadows, Trump's Chief of Staff, and six others test positive for COVID-19
description_medium: Mark Meadows, then White House chief of staff, and six others tested positive for COVID-19 in early November 2020. News of Meadows’s diagnosis broke late Friday, after Election Day. Reports said he began telling staff after initial election results appeared on Tuesday, though it was unclear when he learned he was infected or whether he had symptoms.
description_long: Mark Meadows, Donald Trump’s chief of staff, and six other people tested positive for COVID-19 in early November 2020. The news about Meadows became public late Friday, November 6, after Election Day. Reports said he began informing staff after initial election results appeared on Tuesday, November 3. They did not establish exactly when he learned he was infected, whether he had symptoms, or when the six other people received their results. The timing placed the diagnosis of a senior White House official during the election period and raised questions about when staff were notified. The account records positive tests and the reported communication timeline; it does not show who infected whom, whether Meadows’s diagnosis affected vote counting, or what precautions were taken by each person. The event should be described as a cluster of reported infections and a delayed public disclosure, with the uncertainty around the diagnosis date kept clear. It is not evidence that the illness changed the election outcome or that Meadows intentionally concealed it.
notes: Repair note: Replaced unrelated election-pressure tags with COVID-19, the White House, and the named people; retained uncertainty about when Meadows learned of the infection.
